title: The Discipline of Using Transitions to Revisit Expectations
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that performance expectations between leaders and team members naturally erode over time through accumulating small assumptions and unstated adjustments. Rather than waiting for a corrective conversation, the newsletter advocates using transition moments (new year, promotion, role change, project shift) as natural occasions to reset expectations. In these moments, team members are psychologically open to recalibration because the context has genuinely changed. Leaders should identify upcoming transitions and deliberately use them as structured conversations about what excellent performance looks like going forward. The discipline is not a single event but a recurring practice that prevents the expectation drift that leads to performance problems.
points: Expectation drift is the silent cause of many performance problems: gaps accumulate through small, unstated assumptions rather than dramatic disagreements.

Transitions create psychological openness for recalibration: when something external has changed (role, team, project), team members are more receptive to new expectations without experiencing the conversation as criticism.
The discipline must be proactive, not reactive: waiting until performance degrades to reset expectations turns a routine conversation into a crisis.
Leaders should actively catalog transitions on the horizon: new years, promotions, project shifts, and role changes are all reset opportunities that most leaders miss.

Expectation clarity benefits both parties: team members who know exactly what is expected are better positioned to deliver, and leaders who articulate expectations clearly have a clearer basis for evaluation.
quotes: Over time, the performance expectations shared by leaders and team members tend to become cloudy and less complete.

Differences in perceptions and expectations accumulate quietly, one small assumption at a time. Eventually, the gap between what a leader expects and what a team member delivers grows wide enough to cause real concern or even damage.

When the calendar turns to a new year, when a team member earns a promotion, when a project schedule changes, or when someone steps into a new role or assignment, something shifts in the psychological landscape.
Ask yourself a simple question: What transition is coming up that could serve as a gateway to resetting expectations? Use the segue to do just that.
Close the gap between expectations and performance. This discipline benefits everyone.
